title: The usefulness of YouTube videos as a source of information in asthma
screen_reason: Abstract-only text. Content analysis of 130 YouTube videos about asthma in which videos were coded against scientific correctness: 'Misleading videos provided at least one scientifically incorrect detail, whereas useful videos contained scientifically correct information', and '65.4% of the videos contained scientifically correct information, whereas 18.5% contained misleading information'. That is a quantitative share of items judged false against an external (scientific) ground truth with a stated denominator, so CONTENT. Extraction is limited to what the abstract supports; the search strategy, coder identity and reliability are not recoverable from this text.

estimates.notes: ABSTRACT-ONLY row: the moderator codings marked below are partly inferred and should be treated as provisional. (a) The abstract's METHODS section is truncated in the recovered text ('METHODS: .'), so the search terms, sort order, number of videos screened and any rank truncation are unknown - denom_selection is therefore left blank rather than guessed at 'curated', although YouTube content analyses of this kind almost always use a top-N search set; an adjudicator with the full text should re-check this field and sampling_frame. (b) year is the PUBLICATION year (J Asthma, 2022, doi 10.1080/02770903.2022.2093218); the data-collection date is not stated. (c) country is not stated; coded Global. (d) breadth coded 'false' because the operational trigger is a scientifically incorrect detail, even though the paper's label for the category is 'misleading'; the threshold is lenient (one incorrect detail flags the whole video). (e) Arithmetic check: 18.5% of 130 = 24.05 and 65.4% of 130 = 85.0, both consistent with integer counts on n = 130. (f) NOTE that 65.4% + 18.5% = 83.9%, leaving 16.1% of videos in neither category; the abstract does not say what that residual is, so the 18.5% may sit inside a three-or-more-category scheme rather than a simple correct/misleading dichotomy.

missed_or_uncertain: Text is an abstract only, so anything in the full paper's tables is invisible here. Not extracted from what IS available: (1) uploader-type shares - '26.6% of videos were uploaded by TV shows and YouTube channels, only 7.7% were uploaded by lung specialists' - are provenance, not veracity, so no rows; (2) 'Although videos from medical professionals had a higher quality than videos from YouTube channels and TV shows, the latter were more popular' and 'Misleading videos had numerically, but not statistically significant higher views compared with useful videos' report no shares or scores, so no QUALITY or EXPOSURE row is derivable - in particular the 100,290,242 total views are never split by veracity, so no share-of-views EXPOSURE estimate exists in this text; (3) the residual 16.1% of videos that are neither 'scientifically correct' nor 'misleading' is unexplained. An adjudicator should retrieve the full text to confirm the search strategy, the number of raters and any reliability statistic, the data-collection dates, and whether a per-view (exposure-weighted) misleading share is reported.

rob.design: CANNOT BE ASSESSED from the available text, which is an abstract only and whose METHODS sentence is truncated in the recovered record. What is recoverable: a cross-sectional content analysis of 130 YouTube videos about asthma (total 100,290,242 views, 29 h 8 min of runtime), classified as 'useful' (scientifically correct information) or 'misleading' (at least one scientifically incorrect detail), with uploader type recorded (26.6% TV shows and YouTube channels, 7.7% lung specialists) and video quality compared across uploader types. NOT reported anywhere in the available text: search terms, sort order, screening flow, inclusion/exclusion criteria, language restriction, country, data-collection dates, number and expertise of raters, blinding, adjudication procedure, and any inter-rater reliability statistic. No probability sampling; no response rate applies.
